No matter how far apart you take them—even if one stays here on Earth and the other gets sent to Mars—the moment you flip one and it lands on heads, the other one instantly becomes tails. They're connected in a way that defies our normal understanding of distance.

In the quantum world, particles like electrons can be entangled so that their properties are correlated. When you measure one particle's spin or polarization, you immediately know what the other one's will be, even though neither had a definite value before you measured it. Einstein called this "spooky action at a distance" because it seemed so strange that information seemed to travel faster than light.

The key thing is that the particles don't actually send signals to each other. They just share a quantum state that means measuring one affects the other instantly. It's been proven in experiments many times, and it's now being used for things like quantum computing and secure communication.
